title: Radio beams
kid: The tower has lots of tiny antennas. Together they aim a beam right at each phone. And every phone gets its own seats in time and in radio colours, like seats on a bus, so they never talk over each other.
nerd: A massive-MIMO panel beamforms a separate beam per user. Each 0.5 ms slot (30 kHz sub-carrier spacing) the scheduler hands out resource blocks: OFDMA shares time and frequency between users, so dozens of phones use the same 100 MHz at once.

describe.kid: A cell tower points glowing beams at three phones, and your phone has a label. Beside them, a grid of tiny seats slides by for time and radio colours. Coloured seats light up for each phone. The matching beam glows when that phone gets a turn.
describe.nerd: The gNB panel beamforms three users while a time-frequency grid scrolls beside it. Coloured resource blocks mark OFDMA allocations. The current slot makes the matching beam brighten. Labels call out 64T64R beamforming, 30 kHz spacing and 0.5 ms slots.

2010.title: One wave, shared codes
2010.kid: The tower sends one wide wave over every phone on its side. The phones take turns, 2 ms at a time, and each turn is split into codes, like voices singing different tunes at once. The more phones watch, the smaller each one’s share.
2010.nerd: WCDMA on one 5 MHz carrier: a sector antenna covers about 120°, with no beamforming. HSDPA shares up to 15 SF16 codes; every 2 ms TTI the NodeB gives them to one or a few UEs, by their CQI. 7.2–14 Mbit/s peak per cell with 16-QAM; a phone got 1–3 Mbit/s in practice.

describe.kid: A cell tower sends one wide wave over three phones, and your phone has a label. Beside them, a grid of tiny seats slides by: rows of codes, columns of 2 ms turns. Each turn’s seats mostly light up for one phone.
describe.nerd: The NodeB’s sector covers three UEs with one wave. A code × time grid scrolls beside it: each 2 ms TTI’s HS-PDSCH codes go to one UE, sometimes split with a second. Labels give the 5 MHz carrier, 15 codes and the 2 ms TTI.
